passage: Dear Bettina, the lighthouse posting is confirmed, and before you organize the family into a rescue party, read to the end. It is not the hermitage you are imagining: the light itself has been automatic since 1990, and my job, officially attendant and guide, is to keep the museum in the old keeper's quarters, run the tours from Easter to October, and record the weather twice daily for the coastal service, which pays a stipend of 180 a month on top of the salary and the house. The house, Bettina. Four rooms, a stove that could heat a church, and every window full of sea. The island has eleven permanent residents, a shop that opens when Margrethe feels the shop should open, a school with, currently, one pupil, and a boat on Mondays and Thursdays, weather permitting, which phrase, I am told, does the work of a whole calendar here. I know what you will say: that I am thirty-eight, that this is running away. I have thought about that on the ferry, in the rain, gladly. It is running toward, and the difference is everything. My predecessor stayed 22 years and left only because her knees could no longer manage the 84 steps, and her parting advice, taped inside the log cupboard, reads: name the seals, not the storms. I have already named three seals. Come in June; the puffins will outnumber your objections. Your unrepentant sister, Karin.
question: On which days does the boat come to the island?

passage: Dear Mr. Okada, you asked me at the funeral, kindly and sideways in the manner of these things, whether I would keep my husband's repair shop open, and I answered something polite and empty because the true answer was not ready. It is ready now, and since your question was the first honest one, you get the first answer: yes, and differently. I cannot mend clocks. Forty years married to the trade and I never learned the escapement from the mainspring, which Georg found restful, having one room in his life without an expert in it. But I kept the books, knew every customer by their clock rather than their name, and understand, better than anyone living, his queue system, the shelf of shame for abandoned repairs, and the drawer of parts he called the orphanage. So: I have hired Dena Kowalczyk, the young woman from the technical school Georg tutored on Saturdays without telling me, though the biscuits went somewhere every week and I can count. She repairs; I run the shop, the books, and the talking, which was always half the trade anyway; and the sign stays exactly as it is, because Georg and Son was wrong for thirty years already, there being no son, and a shop that has survived one lie of signage can survive the truth. We reopen on the first Monday of March. Bring the walnut regulator; he left notes on it, three pages, and Dena has read them like scripture. Warmly, Hanne Vogel.
question: Who has the writer hired to do the repairs?

passage: Dear Cousin Emmett, you asked what actually happened at the family reunion, having wisely stayed away, and everyone else will give you their faction's version, so here is the neutral report from the only person who spent the whole day in the kitchen and heard all sides through the hatch. The famous argument was not about the will at all, whatever your mother tells you; the will was settled by four in the afternoon with less fuss than the seating plan. The eruption was about the recipe. Great-aunt Sofie's plum dumpling recipe, which three branches of this family have each claimed as sole inheritance for twenty years, turns out to exist in her own handwriting, dated, in the cookery notebook Uncle Casimir found in the sideboard he inherited and never opened, and the handwriting settles it: the recipe is titled, in her own letters, for the whole tribe, no hoarding, underlined twice. You could hear the silence from the kitchen. Then your Aunt Rilla laughed first, which history should record to her credit, and by evening all three branches were in my kitchen making one enormous batch under the notebook propped open against the radio, arguing only about whether the dough rests 30 minutes or an hour, which the notebook, with what I can only call foresight, does not say. Fourteen dozen dumplings. No casualties. The notebook goes to the town archive, photocopies to everyone. Your loving cousin, Berthe.
question: What is the plum dumpling recipe titled in Sofie's own handwriting?
answer: for the whole tribe, no hoarding

passage: Dear Professor Lindgren, you will remember me, I hope, as the mature student in the back row of your Tuesday evening geology class, the one who asked too many questions about the local quarry. This letter is a confession of what those questions were for, now that the matter is public. My family has argued for three generations about why the well at our farm, dug by my great-grandfather in 1902, gives soft water while every neighbor's well within a mile gives hard, an oddity that cost my grandfather two friendships and one lawsuit, the neighbors suspecting, variously, trickery, divine favor, and an illegal pipe. Your lecture on the valley's buried gravels, the old river channel you drew on the board in yellow chalk, sat in my head for a week before I understood: our farm sits on your yellow line. I wrote to the county geological survey, enclosed the well log my great-grandfather kept in pencil in the family Bible, and their reply, framed this Christmas and hung above the fireplace where the argument used to live, confirms the well draws from the buried channel sands, rainwater filtered through gravel, while the neighbors draw from the limestone. No trickery, no favor, no pipe: an old river, minding its own business under four farms. My mother cried. The neighbor, the lawsuit one's grandson, came to see the letter and stayed for supper. You taught a night class; you settled 120 years of family weather. With respect, Signe Holt.
question: In what year was the farm's well dug?

passage: Dear Wilhelmina, the auction is done, and the bookshop's last chapter closed at four in the afternoon with the fall of a hammer I had dreaded for a year and, when it came, minded less than I expected, which is the first of several surprises this letter contains. The stock went in 214 lots over two days. The county library took the local history shelf entire, lot 1, as I had quietly arranged, and paid properly. The surprise: lot 190, the box of unsold poetry pamphlets I nearly threw away in the packing, local poets, forty years of them, fetched 900 dollars from a collector who drove four hours and told me, while wrapping them himself in his own paper, that half those poets exist nowhere else, and that booksellers like me had been, his words, the unpaid archive of the province. I sat down after he left. The shelves themselves, the oak ones your grandfather built in 1961, went to the new bakery on Cathedral Lane, where they will hold bread, which I find I approve of; bread and books have always been the same argument about what a town owes itself. I kept back one thing, against all auction rules: the first book I ever sold, a botany, bought back over the years three times from three house clearances like a homing bird. It is on my kitchen table. I am 74, solvent, and free on Tuesdays for the first time since the war ended. Teach me chess. Your friend, Gustav.
question: How much did the box of poetry pamphlets fetch?

passage: Dear Nell, your mother tells me you are discouraged about the garden after the slugs took your first sowing, and she suggested, in the way mothers arrange these things, that a letter from your great-uncle might land better than her sympathy, so here is what fifty years of vegetables have taught me, in the order I wish someone had told me. First: everyone loses the first sowing. Everyone, every year. I lose one still, and I have a system, a reputation, and a mortar of dried eggshells. Sow three times: one for the slugs, one for the weather, one for the table, and when all three grow, which some insulting year will happen, give the surplus away and take the credit. Second: your soil is new and so are you; grow this year what wants to grow, radishes, beans, potatoes in a sack, and let them teach you the watering before you attempt the divas, by which I mean celery and everything in the cabbage tribe. Third, the one that matters: keep a notebook, dated, honest, including the failures, especially the failures. Mine begins in 1974 with the words all lettuce dead, cause unknown, and that notebook is now the most useful book in my house, and I include the dictionary. The slugs, by the way: beer traps are folklore that works, torchlight at ten at night works better, and ducks work best, but negotiate with your mother before pursuing the duck solution, and do not cite me as precedent. Sow again this weekend. Your fellow gardener, Uncle Piet.
question: With what words does the great-uncle's notebook begin?

passage: Dear Mr. Fairhurst, I am writing to you as the last chairman of the Ottersby brass band, dissolved, as you will remember painfully, in 2011, because something has happened that the remaining members deserve to hear from me rather than the newspaper. A young woman named Priya Chowdhury, who moved to Ottersby three years ago and plays the cornet, found our old band room behind the fire station while looking for storage for her kayak, and found with it the instruments, all 26 of them, which we could never bring ourselves to sell and which have slept in their cases under the dust sheets since the final concert. She did not find them as junk. She found them, she told me across my own kitchen table with the case of the solo cornet open between us like an argument, as a band, waiting. She has done the arithmetic: eleven of the old members still in the district and able, by her canvass, which she conducted before ever knocking on my door, nine willing, and enough newcomers from the estates, where the town has grown, to fill the stands if the old hands will teach. She asks nothing of me but the constitution documents and my blessing. She is getting both, and the key, and, God help me, my euphonium from under the stairs, which my wife has promised to witness. First rehearsal is the second Thursday of September, seven sharp, the old room. Come and sit in the back with me, deaf and delighted. Yours, Stanley Broome.
question: How many of the old instruments were found in the band room?

passage: My dear Astrid, I have taken up swimming in the sea, in winter, at the age of 71, and since you are the only one of my children who will not immediately telephone a doctor, you are the one who gets the letter about it. It began in October, as a dare from Vibeke at the funeral of poor Solvej, who we agreed would have found our black coats and dry eyes ridiculous; Vibeke said the two of us should do one absurd brave thing before our own turns came, and the sea was at the bottom of the churchyard hill, and grief makes its own logic. We have gone every morning since, 40 mornings and counting, from the ladder by the old pilot jetty, never alone, never longer than four minutes when the water fell below 8 degrees, which are Vibeke's rules, she having read a pamphlet and appointed herself admiral. What I can report: the cold is not the enemy, the hesitation is; the sea has been warmer than the air since November, a fact nobody believes until the ladder; and there is a moment, at the second breath, when the body stops arguing and something very old in it starts to laugh. We are eleven swimmers now, the youngest 58, the oldest 79, and the harbormaster, who watched us for weeks with binoculars and disapproval, brought us a thermos on Sunday and stayed. Your mother is quite well, better than in years, and completely mad, and both of these on purpose. Come at Christmas and bring your courage. Mama.
question: From where do the swimmers enter the sea?
answer: the ladder by the old pilot jetty

passage: Dear Board of the Millfield Preservation Trust, please accept this letter with the enclosed cheque for 31,000 dollars, and the explanation, which the sum requires and the giver's death permits. I am the executor of the estate of Miss Edith Cranmore, who died in March aged 94, and who was known to most of Millfield, I am aware, as the difficult woman at the end of Sexton Row who fed crows, opposed every carnival, and wrote letters to this trust objecting, over the years, to the color of the mill door, the wording of the mill plaque, and, memorably, the angle of the weathervane. The bequest is for the waterwheel restoration, and it comes with her reason, which she dictated to me in the hospice with her usual precision and made me read back twice. She worked in the mill office from 1948 to 1953, before the flood closed it. The wage clerk in those years, a Mr. Aldous Penn, quietly advanced her two months of pay when her father's illness would have cost the family their house, an irregularity that could have cost him his post, and refused all repayment except a promise: that she would, in her time, put the money where the town could not lose it. She waited seventy years because, in her words, interest should mean something. The weathervane, she wished the board informed, is still four degrees off true. Faithfully, R. Cobbold, solicitor.
question: What is the bequest of 31,000 dollars for?

passage: Dear Jonas, write this date down: the third of June. Because on the third of June, at seventeen minutes past six in the morning, on the 1,462nd day of the attempt, by my log, which you have mocked and which history will vindicate, a swift went into the tower. Not over it, not around it, into it, through the east opening, the one you and I widened with the borrowed scaffold in the rain in 2021 while your wife documented our incompetence from the dry side of the window. Four years, Jonas. Four years of playing their screaming calls off the speaker every dawn in season, of adjusting the openings by centimeters on the advice of a man in another country who studies nothing else, of the neighbors' patience and the vicar's raised eyebrow, since the tower is, after all, his church's, and of your annual suggestion, delivered every August like a bill, that the birds had voted with their wings. She stayed forty minutes. She came back twice before noon, and at dusk, Jonas, there were two of them, screaming round the spire with the flock and cutting in through the east opening one after the other like thread through a needle, and I stood in the churchyard with the log book against my chest like a fool at a miracle. Nesting is not proven. I know the cautions, I wrote the cautions. But the vicar has already asked what year we shall paint on the commemorative tile, and I have permitted myself to answer: this one. Your friend, entirely vindicated, Old Matthias.
question: Through which opening did the swift enter the tower?
distractors: the dry side of the window
